item.title: Jaguars are first team since the merger not to allow a 40-yard rusher in first five games
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Opposing running backs have 83 carries for 210 yards against the Jaguars this season, an average of just 2.5 yards per carry.
item.content:encoded:
No one can run the ball on the Jaguars.

Through five games this season, the most rushing yards any player has gained in a game against the Jaguars was 39, by Broncos running back Jonah Coleman.. That makes the Jaguars the first team since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger not to allow an opposing player to rush for 40 or more yards in the first five games of a season.

The last team not to allow a 40-yard rusher in the first five games was the 1969 Cowboys.

Last year, the most rushing yards any player gained in a game against the Jaguars was 74, by Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. The Jaguars have now gone 23 consecutive games, counting last year's playoff game, without allowing a 75-yard rusher.

Opposing running backs have totaled 83 carries for 210 yards against the Jaguars this season, an average of just 2.5 yards per carry. That's by far the best defense against running backs in the NFL this season.

On Sunday in London the Jaguars face the Texans, who rank 31st in the league with 395 rushing yards this season.

item.title: Al Michaels won't complain if Prime Video wants to move on
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The legendary Al Michaels continues to call the biggest of NFL games, four decades after making his debut on Monday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
The legendary Al Michaels continues to call the biggest of NFL games, four decades after making his debut on Monday Night Football. Now in his fifth year with Thursday Night Football on Prime Video, the 81-year-old broadcasting icon realizes that, at some point, it will end.

Appearing on Wednesday's edition of The Dan Patrick Show, Michaels addressed the question of when he'll know the time has come.

“Well, either the people that I work for will tell me, or I’ll know myself, a combination,” Michaels said, via Sam Neumann of Awful Announcing. “Let’s put it this way. The folks at Amazon and Prime have been fantastic. Fantastic to me.”

After his initial three-year deal, Prime Video has extended the arrangement on a one-year basis, twice. If they don't do it again, Michaels will be fine with that.

“If they come to me and say, 'You know, it’s time for us to move on.' . . . 'You guys have been fantastic. You’ve been great.' I’ve done the NFL for 41 years, which is half my life. Love it. But you know what? At a certain time, it’s time. And if they feel it’s time, great. And if I feel it’s time, I’ll know it. And I’ll say, ‘You know what? Thanks for the memories.'"

We're the ones who should be thanking him. As we've said before, many won't appreciate how much of our sports-watching lives he has influenced until he's no longer part of it. And while there are plenty of highly competent voices out there, Michaels is one of the very best to ever do it — possibly the best of all of the play-by-play announcers.

He has been able to land in a high-profile spot after his tenure at NBC ended before he likely wanted it to. We've been able to listen to him call games for another four-plus years, thanks to the fact that Prime Video hired him.

So either he'll walk away or he'll get a nudge. Either way, Michaels's long and distinguished journey has much greater meaning than however the road ends. For me and many others, it won't be the same to go through a football season without hearing him calling a game every week.

item.title: Jalen Hurts won't say much about "very unique" calf injury that was disclosed last Friday
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Last week's injury report for the Eagles included a curious designation on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Last week's injury report for the Eagles included a curious designation on Friday. And Wednesday's comments from the player at the center of the issue served only to make it more curious.

Quarterback Jalen Hurts was listed as fully participating in Friday's practice before the game against the Jaguars with a calf injury. He had no injury designation for Sunday's game in London, and he was never downgraded to questionable or doubtful.

When the question came up during his midweek press conference, here's what Hurts said: "It was a very unique experience, to say the least. I don't want to get into the details of kind of leading up to the game and whatnot, but got nicked up in the Rams game."

There's a lot there, in not that many words. What would be "very unique" about a calf injury that didn't impact his practice reps? And why would it be a big secret?

The complicating factor is that the Eagles flew to London on Friday. Did he require medical care in London? Would it be something that the team doctors were able to provide? Did he have to visit a local hospital for it?

He said he was "nicked up" during the Rams game, but he wasn't on the injury report for Wednesday or Thursday. Was is it that could have happened on Sunday that would have resulted in symptoms on Friday. (A condition like compartment syndrome typically surfaces much more quickly.)

Regardless, plenty of questions flow from what seems to be very innocuous and basic on the surface. Hurts's words deepen the mystery.

He remains on the Week 6 injury report, in advance of Sunday's game against the Panthers. Hurts was listed as a full participant in Wednesday's practice, due to the calf injury.

Whatever the explanation is, there's clearly more to the story than what the team has disclosed. And the NFL doesn't require much more than the bare-bones contents of the injury report.
